A status command expresses a desired value. If a legal case tracker record is already Discovery, setting it to Discovery again is not another business event. Compare the current value before writing. A date such as 2028-02-29 is a calendar label. Validate its shape and compare its parsed calendar components; 2027-02-29 has the right shape but is not a real day. Activity timestamps are instants and have different semantics. Amounts are bounded nonnegative currency values; a fractional cent is rejected rather than silently rounded. This scaffold does not perform external billing, legal work, dispatch integration or research compliance checks.

A stable sort needs a secondary key. With several equal timestamps, ID determines the remaining order. Count matching records after filters, calculate the last page, clamp the request, then fetch that page. Synchronous array operations cannot interleave midway through an await because there is no await in that boundary. This explanation is specific to one process. Add a reason to an actual status transition.
Test deletion of the final row on a filtered last page.

Validate a bounded reason and save it with the transition event. A same-value command should not invent another transition.
Create three matching records with size two, delete the last row and request the old page. Assert both the returned page number and matching IDs.

Return a version number and require the expected version on update. Reject stale writes with a clear conflict response; keep the learner draft available for comparison. Row locking alone does not detect an edit based on an old screen.

title: Warehouse Ledger: transactions and derived stock
focus: protecting a balance under concurrent writes
before: Fractional quantities were truncated, and two transactions could both read enough stock before either wrote its debit.
after: Movement and transfer payloads require valid UUIDs, bounded whole quantities and text reasons. Every write locks the product before reading balances. Transfers remain two atomic ledger entries.
model: Products and warehouses have UUIDs. A movement references one of each and carries signed integer delta, reason and creation time. Stock is SUM(delta) per product/warehouse; there is no separately stored balance to synchronize.
concept:
An append-only ledger represents corrections with new entries. Receiving 10 adds +10; issuing 3 adds -3; the balance is 7. A transfer adds -q at the source and +q at the destination, so total stock across warehouses is conserved. Deleting a movement to correct a mistake would erase the explanation of how stock arrived at its current value.

A transaction makes multiple writes all-or-nothing, but a transaction alone does not prevent two readers from approving the same stock. This app locks a product row before computing balances. All movement and transfer writers use that same lock. One product lock serializes its warehouses, trading some concurrency for an understandable rule and avoiding inconsistent lock order between opposite transfers. Direct SQL writers that ignore this protocol are outside the application guarantee.

Number.isInteger checks the quantity rather than truncating it. A request for 1.7 units must not quietly become one unit. The bound matches the SQL integer column. The product lock is taken even for receipts so all writers participate in one ordering. Warehouse existence is checked before inserts; SQL foreign keys still protect stored references.
example: The seeded cable stock is 40 at Main. Send two concurrent issues of 30: one succeeds, one is rejected, and the balance is 10. Force the destination credit of a transfer to fail: neither debit nor credit remains. A valid transfer of 3 leaves total stock unchanged.
exercises: Display a running balance in the ledger.
Add a reversal command referencing the original movement.
Reject a transfer when one warehouse is missing and show recovery feedback.
Compare per-product locking with per-product/warehouse locking.
answers: Order movements by timestamp and a stable tie-breaker, then accumulate deltas. Explain that the visible 100-row window may require an opening balance.
Create an opposite signed movement in a transaction and store the original ID. Prevent a repeated reversal from duplicating the effect.
Assert no new rows on failure, retain the form and explain which reference is missing.
Finer locks improve concurrency but transfers require both locks in a deterministic order. Include opposing transfers in a deadlock test before adopting that design.

title: Secure Notes: owned CRUD and runtime boundaries
focus: authorizing records and rejecting malformed JSON
before: Object-valued credentials and note fields could reach string or password operations. Reading a single owned note had no dedicated endpoint.
after: Credentials and note text are typed and bounded, email normalization is consistent, and an owned note detail endpoint completes the read path. Owner checks protect read, update and delete; logout revokes its token.
model: Users and tokens are Maps; notes are an array with id, userId, title, body and createdAt. A Bearer token selects a user. Passwords are salted and hashed with scrypt. All data and sessions disappear on server restart.
concept:
Authentication asks which user the request represents. Authorization asks whether that user may access this note. Finding a note by ID alone is insufficient: the owner predicate must also match. Returning the same 404 for a missing and another user's note keeps the response consistent. The test signs in as two different users and tries each operation rather than merely inspecting the middleware name.

TypeScript is not involved in this JavaScript server, and even TypeScript types would not validate network JSON. A password object must fail before scryptSync. Email normalization trims and lowercases before looking up the same map key for register and login. Passwords are not trimmed, because spaces are part of the user's chosen credential.

The title has a 2–200 character rule; the body is text up to 20,000 characters. Validation happens before the note mutates. This is a small authentication teaching app, with in-memory sessions, open CORS and synchronous hashing. Persistent accounts, rate limits, session expiration and deployment configuration remain separate improvements.
example: User A creates Learning note. User B sees an empty note list and receives 404 for A's detail, edit and delete paths. An invalid body leaves the old note intact. After A logs out, the old token receives 401.
exercises: Show an explicit empty-note state after login.
Add a last-edited timestamp that changes only after a valid update.
Test a failed login followed by a successful login.
Move users, tokens and notes into persistent storage.
answers: Distinguish an empty successful list from a failed request; do not display no notes while authentication is still loading.
Keep createdAt stable and set updatedAt only at the successful mutation boundary. Test rejected edits do not touch it.
Keep the generic invalid-credentials response and confirm a malformed input does not terminate the process.
Create owner foreign keys, use parameterized queries and keep owner predicates on every record operation. Design session expiration and password hashing capacity explicitly.

title: Live Chat: validate before broadcasting
focus: HTTP boundaries, WebSocket messages and database notifications
before: Malformed socket events could call trim on nonstrings; listener startup occurred during import and asynchronous failures could escape their handlers.
after: Room fields and socket messages are validated. Runtime start/stop functions enable isolated tests; malformed messages are ignored, database failures close the affected socket, and the payload size is bounded.
model: Rooms have id, slug and name. Messages have id, roomId, author, body and createdAt. WebSockets subscribe to room IDs, while PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY delivers committed message notifications to the process.
concept:
A WebSocket remains open across many messages. One bad JSON message should not kill the process or prevent the next valid message. Parsing JSON checks syntax; checking type, author and body checks the protocol shape. A maximum frame payload bounds memory use independently from field-length validation.

The write path inserts into PostgreSQL. A database trigger produces a notification, the dedicated LISTEN connection receives it, and the process broadcasts to sockets in that room. This is a different path from returning an HTTP response. The integration test waits for a real message broadcast and then reads HTTP history to confirm persistence.

Starting listeners at module import makes tests unexpectedly bind ports and retain database connections. Explicit lifecycle functions put those side effects under caller control. stopRuntime terminates sockets, closes the server and listener, and clears a scheduled retry. The current reconnection attempt is bounded teaching behavior, not a durable delivery guarantee: disconnected clients recover recent history, not an acknowledged message queue. Author names remain free-form demo labels, not authenticated users.
example: Connect to study, wait for presence, send malformed JSON, null, and an object-valued author, then send Trace this insert. The valid message broadcasts and appears once in HTTP history. Creating study twice returns 409.
exercises: Show a sending/error state for a message draft.
Add a room rename endpoint without changing the room ID or slug.
Test two rooms to ensure broadcasts do not cross subscriptions.
Design acknowledged delivery and reconnect replay.
answers: Introduce a client message ID and an acknowledgement protocol; retain the draft until accepted. Do not infer durable storage merely from socket.send returning.
Validate the new display name and update only that field; existing messages retain their room foreign key.
Open a socket in each room, send one message and assert only the matching room receives it. Close both sockets in finally.
Use persistent message IDs and a replay cursor. Explain duplicates, ordering and acknowledgement loss before claiming exactly-once delivery.

title: Survey Builder: valid answers and response capacity
focus: nested validation and atomic response submission
before: Unknown choices, empty required arrays and invalid ratings could be stored. Opening dates were not checked and the response limit was checked before the transaction.
after: Public reads and submissions enforce opening windows and capacity. Submission locks the survey, validates answers against its questions, writes response/answers and increments the counter in one transaction. Optional blank ratings stay null.
model: A user owns surveys. A survey has questions, each with a question_type and optional choice rows/config. A response belongs to a survey; response_answers reference that response and its questions. response_count is a stored aggregate that must match accepted submissions.
concept:
Validation is a relationship problem here. A string can be valid text but an invalid choice for this question. Load the question definitions and check answer keys, requiredness, types and allowed choices before writing. A multi-choice array must contain known labels; deduplicate repeated selections. An optional blank rating means no answer, not zero. A required matrix must include each configured row and only configured columns.

The response counter is a second mutable fact. Insert the response and all its answers, then increment the counter using the same transaction. A late error must undo the earlier inserts. Capacity adds a concurrency rule: lock the survey row before checking response_count, so two requests cannot both take the last slot. The transaction reads the questions through the same connection.

The date window compares instants, unlike the domain apps' date-only fields. At the end timestamp the survey is closed. The access code is checked inside the submission transaction. The app still uses a demo owner header for administrative routes. Concurrent editing of question definitions and full administrative authorization deserve their own design; this change focuses on response acceptance.
example: A required multi-choice question accepts JavaScript once even if it appears twice in the submitted array. Unknown, object and empty answers return 400 and create no response. Two submissions to max_responses=1 produce one 201 and one 400. Future, expired and closed surveys reject submissions.

Add an answer-preview table before submission.
Force the second answer insert to fail and verify the whole response rolls back.
Define a policy for editing a question after responses exist.
answers: Map question IDs to errors without replacing the respondent draft; keep the server check authoritative.
Build a read-only projection of the draft. Do not count a preview as a response or increment the counter.
Use a disposable-schema trigger and assert response rows, answer rows and counter all equal their pre-request values.

title: Polling Chat: scope every conversation operation
focus: membership predicates and shared route guards
before: History, polling, reactions and group-management routes did not consistently verify membership. A duplicate member ID could break group creation.
after: A shared route guard verifies the demo user's membership for conversation/message operations, restricts group management to admins and validates read-receipt references. Group creation deduplicates members.
model: Users join conversations through conversation_members, whose role is admin/member. Messages reference a conversation and author. Reactions reference a message and user. Read receipts store last_read_message_id on membership rows; typing indicators also reference conversation/user.
concept:
A foreign key proves that a referenced row exists, not that the caller is allowed to see it. The route guard resolves a message to its conversation and checks the membership pair (conversation_id,user_id). This covers GET history, GET polling, POST reactions and metadata operations with the same rule. Owner checks still decide who may edit a particular message.

A read receipt is not merely any existing message ID. It must belong to the conversation being marked read, or unread calculations become misleading. An administrator role is likewise scoped to the membership row for that conversation; being an admin in another group grants nothing here. The x-demo-user-id header is still freely chosen in this educational app, so this demonstrates authorization structure without providing real authentication.

Polling retrieves messages after a cursor. Membership must be checked on every poll, not only when the UI first opens a room, because membership can change. This central check is a useful boundary, but it is not a transaction spanning every subsequent read; strict coordination with simultaneous membership removal would need additional policy and locking.
example: User 3 cannot read or poll the study room, react to its messages, type there or add members. User 2 can read and react but cannot manage members. A receipt pointing to another room is rejected. The author can edit/delete a message; a deleted message cannot be revived by editing.

Test polling after removing a user from a group.

title: Team Project Management: lifecycle and bulk edits
focus: preserving workflow state and atomic multi-record changes
before: Restore always assigned active, even when that was not a valid workflow state. Bulk updates could silently ignore missing IDs and audit entries lacked the actual previous record.
after: Archive stores the previous status in an additive migration, restore returns to that status, and repeats are no-ops. Ordinary and bulk status changes keep archive flags consistent. Bulk IDs are deduplicated; all targets are locked and checked before any change. Audit rows contain real before/after records. List refreshes ignore stale responses and use the current filters after a mutation; failed saves retain the draft and show an error.
model: tasks belong to the grouping reference workspace_id. Records have title, owner, priority, status, metadata, due_at, risk_level, version, archived_at and deleted_at. Status vocabulary: todo, in_progress, blocked, done, archived. The new nullable status_before_archive column remembers the earlier state. Comments, activity_events and audit_log reference records.
concept:

A legacy archived row without the new saved field falls back to todo; the migration does not invent a historical state it cannot know.

It deduplicates IDs before comparing lengths, locks targets in ID order and skips rows already at the desired status. Every changed record receives an audit entry with the actual previous and resulting values. A misleading before:null would make it harder to explain what changed.

The server validates partial fields before writing and keeps IDs stable. The version increments on change, but this is not yet optimistic concurrency: a client does not send an expected version. A row lock serializes writes; it does not detect a stale full-form edit. The role header is a demo mechanism, and workspace_id is a grouping foreign key rather than an enforced tenant boundary. Bulk-update [existingId,999999]: return 404 and leave the existing row unchanged. A duplicated valid ID changes once and audit.before/status differs from audit.after/status.
exercises: Display the previous status while a record is archived.
Preview the distinct IDs affected by a bulk action.
Inject an audit-write failure and verify all bulk changes roll back.
Add optimistic concurrency and genuine authorization.
answers: Read status_before_archive and label a missing legacy value honestly; do not infer an earlier state from the current badge.
Deduplicate selected IDs and show the exact target count. Keep server validation for removed or stale IDs.

title: Recipeview: validate a nested edit before replacing children
focus: parent-child CRUD, partial edits and SQLite transactions
before: Nested recipe payloads could contain malformed ingredient/step values, blank edits were silently ignored, and IDs/dates were accepted by loose conversions.
after: A shared request boundary rejects malformed nested values and noncanonical IDs before handlers mutate rows. Recipe edits retain omitted children; valid replacements and search reindexing remain transactional. The app can be imported without binding a development port.
model: Dishes own recipes. Recipes own ordered ingredients, steps and cook logs; logs can own photos. Tags and the search_index support discovery. SQLite stores relationships; photo files live separately under RECIPE_LAB_DATA/photos.
concept:
A recipe editor often submits a complete ingredient list, so replacing children can be easier to understand than diffing each row. That design is safe only when validation and transaction boundaries are clear. Omitting ingredients means preserve them; sending [] means intentionally remove all. Reject a malformed row before deleting the old children, so a typo does not erase an otherwise valid recipe.

Search is another representation of the same domain data. Renaming a recipe updates its searchable context through reindexRecipeTree. The SQL transaction includes the parent edit, child replacement and search-index writes. Photo files cannot participate in a SQLite transaction, so deletion collects filenames before the database cascade and removes files after commit. A file-removal failure requires separate cleanup policy.

A quantity is a number or a deliberate blank, not an arbitrary object coerced to zero. The browser parses kitchen fractions before sending JSON. The API validates nonnegative ingredient quantities and positive recipe yield. Canonical positive integer IDs reject strings such as 1e2 rather than interpreting them as another record. This remains a local personal recipe app without multi-user authorization.
example: Create Pasta with a Weeknight recipe, one ingredient and one step. PATCH only title: both child lists remain. Send title Changed with a negative ingredient quantity: return 400 and preserve parent, children and search data. Deleting the dish cascades its recipes and removes their search entries.

Compute quantity times desiredYield/originalYield as derived state. Keep the saved recipe unchanged until a separate edit is confirmed.
Use a fresh SQLite fixture and trigger failure after the parent update; assert the title and children retain their prior values.
Replace wholesale deletion with explicit create/update/delete operations keyed by ingredient ID. Explain ordering independently from identity and add conflict handling for concurrent editors.

focus: runtime schemas, nested records and import boundaries
before: Backup parsing checked only outer arrays/settings presence, so malformed events, recurrence, application history or duplicate IDs could reach the stores.
after: Backup parsing validates supported version, settings, category/event/application IDs, real dates, recurrence bounds, nested history and salary relationships before approving replacement.
model: The browser stores calendar events, categories, job applications and settings with Zustand/localStorage. Events can recur and reference job IDs. Applications have a current stage plus StageChange history. A Backup contains all four stores, app marker, version and exportedAt.

Casting JSON to Backup tells TypeScript to trust the programmer; it does not inspect the file. A valid outer object can still contain events:[null] or recurrence.interval=0. The latter can break recurrence generation or create excessive work. Validate nested values at the import boundary before passing them to any replaceAll action.

Duplicate IDs are a data-integrity problem even when every individual row is otherwise valid. React keys, store updates and references all rely on identity. The validator checks uniqueness within each record collection and each application history. It validates real calendar dates and increasing local event times without converting local appointments into UTC instants. An unknown category ID remains compatible with the existing display fallback.

The parser is pure: it returns either a validated backup or an error. Purity makes malformed cases easy to test without touching storage. Actual replacement still spans multiple localStorage-backed stores; validating first prevents malformed input from causing partial replacement, but a quota failure during later writes is a separate atomicity problem. A future redesign could store one versioned document or use one IndexedDB transaction.

after: Blank optional edits explicitly clear nullable fields, omitted fields remain unchanged, blank salaries remain null, and real dates are validated. Partial update has three meanings: omitted means keep the old value, null means clear it, and a concrete value means replace it. An empty HTML text input is a string, so the boundary must map it deliberately. Cross-field validation belongs after merging a partial update with stored data. A request containing only salary_max=50 can violate the saved salary_min=100 even if the request schema sees only one field. The existing merged salary guard is retained and tested. Real YYYY-MM-DD validation compares the parsed label, so February 30 cannot silently roll into March.

A status command sets a desired state. Repeating the current state now returns that same record without updating updated_at. Other transitions still use ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS. This is a narrow retry guarantee; POST creation still needs a separate idempotency design. JWT ownership checks remain on every application path.
